subject: chem
title: Reaction Kinetics
subtitle: Rate of reaction, activation energy and catalysis.
concept: Reaction rate depends on collision frequency and collision energy — collisions must exceed the activation energy (Ea) to be successful.
Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution shows the spread of molecular energies; only molecules to the right of Ea react.
Catalysts provide an alternative reaction pathway with lower Ea, increasing the proportion of successful collisions without being consumed.

notes.heading: Factors Affecting Rate
items: Concentration: more particles per unit volume → more frequent collisions → faster rate.
Temperature: increases average kinetic energy AND fraction of molecules with E ≥ Ea; even a 10°C rise roughly doubles rate.
Surface area: more exposed particles available for collisions.
Catalyst: lowers Ea, increasing fraction of successful collisions.

notes.heading: Maxwell–Boltzmann Distribution
items: X-axis: kinetic energy. Y-axis: number of molecules (proportion) with that energy.
Area under curve = total number of molecules (constant).
Most probable energy is the peak; mean energy is slightly to the right.
Ea marked as a vertical line; area to the right = molecules that can react.
Higher T: curve flattens and shifts right; Ea line stays fixed; shaded area increases greatly.
Catalyst: lowers Ea to Ea'; shaded area increases without changing temperature.

notes.heading: Catalysis
items: Homogeneous catalyst: same phase as reactants (e.g. H⁺(aq) in ester hydrolysis).
Heterogeneous catalyst: different phase (e.g. Fe in Haber process; Pt/Rh in catalytic converters).
Catalysts increase rate but do not change ΔH or the equilibrium position.
Autocatalysis: product of reaction acts as catalyst (e.g. Mn²⁺ in MnO₄⁻ + C₂O₄²⁻ reaction).

definitions.body: Change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹).
The minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur.
A graph showing the distribution of kinetic energies among molecules in a gas at a given temperature.
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction by providing an alternative pathway of lower activation energy, without being consumed.

workedExamples.q: Explain, using the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, why increasing temperature increases reaction rate.

steps.text: At higher T, the curve shifts to the right and becomes broader/flatter; the peak moves to higher energy.
The activation energy Ea stays at the same position on the x-axis.
A much greater proportion of molecules now have energy ≥ Ea, so more collisions are successful per unit time → rate increases significantly.

mistakes: Saying a catalyst 'lowers activation energy of the reaction' without specifying it provides an alternative pathway.
Drawing the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve starting above zero on the y-axis (it must start at origin).
Confusing rate of reaction with extent of reaction — a catalyst changes rate but not equilibrium.
tips: When drawing the effect of a catalyst on Maxwell–Boltzmann: keep the curve identical, just move the Ea line to the left (lower Ea).
For temperature effect: redraw the curve (flatter, right-shifted), keep Ea fixed, shade the new larger area.
Rate units are mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ — always quote them.

flashcards.q: What two factors determine whether a collision is successful?
flashcards.a: The collision must have sufficient energy (≥ Ea) and the correct orientation.

flashcards.q: How does a catalyst increase reaction rate?
flashcards.a: By providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, increasing the fraction of molecules with sufficient energy.
A graph of the distribution of kinetic energies of molecules at a given temperature; area under curve = total molecules.

flashcards.q: What happens to the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution at higher temperature?
flashcards.a: The curve flattens and shifts right (higher average energy); more molecules exceed Ea.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts?
flashcards.a: Homogeneous: same phase as reactants. Heterogeneous: different phase.
No — a catalyst lowers Ea but does not change the enthalpy change of the reaction.

opts: Minimum energy for a successful collision
Average kinetic energy of reactant molecules
questions.exp: Activation energy is the minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur.

questions.q: How does increasing concentration increase rate?
opts: Increases proportion of molecules above Ea
questions.exp: More particles per unit volume → more frequent collisions.

questions.q: A catalyst is added to a reaction. Which is NOT changed?
questions.exp: A catalyst lowers Ea and provides a new pathway, increasing rate — but ΔH is unchanged.

questions.q: On a Maxwell–Boltzmann diagram, what does the area to the right of Ea represent?
opts: Molecules with energy ≥ Ea that can react
questions.exp: The shaded area to the right of the Ea line represents the fraction of molecules with enough energy to react.

questions.q: Iron is used as a catalyst in the Haber process. What type of catalysis is this?
questions.exp: Iron (solid) is a different phase from the gaseous N₂ and H₂ reactants — heterogeneous catalysis.
